newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sales lackluster in October, inflation tame.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sales lackluster in October, inflation tame.

text.p: Tight-fisted consumers spent slightly more in October than they did the previous month, the government reported Thursday, prompting analysts to say the holiday shopping season may be less robust than expected.
Consumers remained frugal despite evidence that inflation at the retail level remained subdued last month, and of continued strength in the job market, separate reports showed.
Retail sales rose a slim 0.2 percent last month, the Commerce Department said, suggesting that the important holiday sales season from Thanksgiving through Christmas may be weaker than anticipated.
Sales by car dealers, department stores, grocery and gasoline stations and other retailers had gained more strongly by 0.8 percent in September.

Separately, the Labour Department said its Consumer Price Index was up 0.3 percent in October, the same as in September. Stripping out volatile food and enery, the so-called core rate of inflation slowed to a 0.2 percent gain from 0.3 percent.

In a third report, the Labour Department confirmed a healthy labour market as new applications for jobless benefits last week dropped 4,000 from a week earlier to 328,000. The four-week average of claims, which smoothes out weekly fluctuations and is considered a more reliable gauge of the labour market, also fell 3,500 to 330,250.
For all the signs of economic strength, though, analysts said the fourth quarter appeared to be starting on a lackluster note with restrained spending by consumers.

"In spite of low unemployment rates, high levels of confidence and solid gains in income, consumers turned cautious during the summer, and that conservative approach has carried into the fall," said economist Joel Naroff of First Union Bank in Charlotte, N.C.
"The fundamentals are there for a robust Christmas rush, but if the psychology has moved in favour of thriftiness, then we may have a more moderate gain in sales this year," Naroff said.

Weaker consumer spending was the key reason for a sharp slowdown in the economy in the third quarter, when gross domestic product eased to a 2.2 percent annual growth rate from a 4.7 percent rate in the second quarter.
Economist David Jones at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co. in New York said the consumer pullback, after a free-spending first half this year, may be part of a healthy long-term trend.

"It's a well-balanced process in which growth is moderate but may be sustainable through next year and beyond," Jones said. "It's a combination of moderate growth and inflation in check that allowed the Fed to keep policy unchanged and will continue to do so on Dec. 17."
Federal Reserve policy-makers held interest rates steady after meeting on Wednesday. They were widely expected to do the same at their final meeting of the year on Dec. 17.
Jones said he still expected a modest pickup, "but not a boom," in consumer spending in November and December.

During October, sales by new-car dealers -- which account for about a quarter of all retail sales -- fell 0.3 percent to $50.7 billion after rising 1.7 percent in September. Excluding cars, retail sales rose 0.4 percent last month after rising 0.5 percent in September.

Moderating economic growth has helped cap inflation, making the job easier for the Fed, which wants to achieve a "soft-landing" of slower growth and contained inflation that will keep the 5-1/2-year-old expansion going.
"Fed Chairman (Alan) Greenspan has hit a home run," Jones said. "He's achieved his soft landing."

The consumer price report showed a continuing rise in food and beverage prices, up 0.6 percent in October after a 0.5 percent September jump. Energy prices rose 0.7 percent after being flat in September. Fuel oil prices jumped 7 percent, the largest rise since an 8.8 percent surge in January.

But Donald Ratajczak, who heads Georgia State University's economic forecasting service, said the worst of the food price rises were over and predicted energy prices will moderate once inventories of winter heating oil are built up.
"This simply isn't an economy that is about to burst with inflationary fervor," Ratajczak said.
